# Tobit Chapter 11 — Disagreement Log
**Arbiter:** SOPHIA | **In council with:** EMET, LOGOS, PNEUMA
**Date:** 2026-03-17

## Overview
Chapter 11 is the climax of Tobit's healing arc. The 19-verse chapter generated 12 significant divergences, concentrated in the approach and reunion sequence (vv. 4-9) and the healing scene proper (vv. 10-13). The central interpretive tension is between PNEUMA's desire to dramatize the climactic moment and the textual discipline maintained by EMET and LOGOS. One key PNEUMA contribution is adopted (v. 11: "steadied his father"). The Anna reunion cry (v. 9) required returning past all three agents to the bare Greek.

---

## Disagreement Table

| Verse | Issue | EMET | LOGOS | PNEUMA | SOPHIA Resolution |
|-------|-------|------|-------|--------|-------------------|
| 11:4 | Dog's movement | "the dog followed after them" | "the dog ran along behind them" | "the dog trotted along behind them" | "the dog ran along behind them" — LOGOS; no warrant for PNEUMA's "trotted" |
| 11:5 | Anna's description | "sitting and looking down the-road" | "sitting and watching the road" | "sitting outside, watching the road, the way she always did" | LOGOS: clean and sufficient; PNEUMA adds three elements not in the text |
| 11:6 | Anna's announcement | "said to his-father" | "called to his father" | "jumped up and called to Tobit" | "called to his father" — LOGOS; "jumped up" has no Greek basis |
| 11:8 | leukōmata | "white-films" | "white films" | "the film that covers them" | "white films" — EMET/LOGOS; the plural and specificity of leukōmata is medically significant |
| 11:9 | Reunion formula | "from now on I can die" | "now I can die in peace" | "now I could die happy" | "now I can die" — bare translation; "in peace" (LOGOS) and "happy" (PNEUMA) both add glosses to an already-complete formula |
| 11:9 | Physical embrace | "fell on the neck-of her-son" | "threw herself on her son's neck" | "threw herself onto her son and held him" | "threw herself on her son's neck" — LOGOS; the neck formula is a specific biblical idiom |
| 11:11 | Sequence of healing actions | "blew-on-it and held-it and applied-it" | "breathed on it, then took hold of his father and applied it" | "breathed on it gently… steadying his father… pressed it" | "breathed on it, then steadied his father and applied it" — SOPHIA conflation: PNEUMA's "steadied" adopted as contextually necessary; "pressed" rejected in favor of "applied" |
| 11:12 | Film detail | "white-films peeled-off from the corners" | "white films peeled away from the corners" | "white film came away — peeling off in pieces" | LOGOS: "peeled away from the corners" — PNEUMA's "in pieces" adds detail not in the Greek |
| 11:13 | Tobit's first sight and embrace | "fell on his-neck and wept" | "fell on his neck and wept" | "grabbed him, held him, and wept" | "fell on his neck and wept" — epepesen epi ton trachēlon autou is a recurring biblical embrace formula (cf. Gen 45:14; Luke 15:20) |
| 11:15 | Tobit's exclamation | "now I see Tobias my-son" | "now I see my son Tobias" | "I am looking at my son Tobias with my own eyes" | "now I see my son Tobias" — LOGOS; PNEUMA's "with my own eyes" is a reasonable but unwarranted expansion |
| 11:17 | Repetition of "my daughter" | bare "daughter" (no possessive) | "my daughter" (full repetition) | Partial reduction | "my daughter" with full repetition — LOGOS; the threefold anaphora is the textual feature |
| 11:18 | Scope of celebration | "all the Jews who were in Nineveh" | "all the Jews in Nineveh" | "every Jewish family in Nineveh" | "all the Jews in Nineveh" — LOGOS; PNEUMA's "every Jewish family" paraphrases the collective |

---

## Extended Notes

### The Anna Reunion Cry (v. 9)
"From now on I can die" (ap' arti apothanō) is one of the most compressed and powerful lines in the chapter. LOGOS added "in peace" — a natural gloss, echoing Luke 2:29 (nunc dimittis). PNEUMA added "happy" — emotionally apt but further from the text. SOPHIA returns to the bare formula: "now I can die." The reader does not need to be told it is peace or happiness; the context — a mother who has been watching the road every day for weeks, weeping every night — supplies all necessary feeling.

### The Healing Sequence (vv. 10-12)
The three-stage healing (breathe on gall / apply to eyes / films peel away) is handled with extraordinary narrative precision by the Greek text. EMET's literal rendering ("blew-on-it and held-it and applied-it") is syntactically heavy but preserves the sequence. LOGOS smooths it. PNEUMA adds "gently" to the breathing, "steadying his father" to the application, and "in pieces" to the peeling — all plausibly realistic but all additions. SOPHIA adopts only "steadied his father," which the scene strongly implies (a blind man stumbling out, his son approaching with medicine) and which adds meaningful narrative detail without embellishing the miraculous.

### The Embrace Formula (v. 13)
"Fell on his neck" (epepesen epi ton trachēlon autou) appears at Gen 45:14 (Joseph and Benjamin), Gen 46:29 (Jacob and Joseph), Luke 15:20 (the prodigal son), and Acts 20:37 (Paul's farewell). It is a specific biblical idiom for reunion embrace. PNEUMA's substitution of "grabbed him, held him" loses this intertextual resonance entirely. SOPHIA preserves the formula.

### The Dog
The dog's return (v. 4) is one of the most discussed details in Tobit scholarship. It appears only twice: at the departure in 6:2 and the return in 11:4. The animal serves no plot function but signals the completeness of the journey — what left, has returned. All three agents include it; the disagreement is only in the verb of movement ("followed," "ran," "trotted"). SOPHIA follows LOGOS: "ran."

*— SOPHIA*
